# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Brouviv Student Transit, Inc. / Droureil Coachways LLC: Pre-closing review of transaction documents

---

## Executive Summary

I reviewed all eight documents in the folder:

- the Asset Purchase Agreement dated August 14, 2026 (APA)
- the form IP Assignment Agreement (IPAA, Exhibit B)
- the side letter dated October 9, 2026
- the Disclosure Schedule
- the form Bill of Sale
- the March 18, 2026 letter of intent (LOI)
- the August 17, 2026 press release
- Brouviv's August 13, 2026 board consent

Closing has not occurred. The APA Outside Date is **December 15, 2026**, which is less than four weeks away. I found five issues that need action before closing. In order of urgency:

| # | Issue | Main location | Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fleet Defect Notice was sent after the 30-day window | Side letter §3; APA §6.8 | $612,000 price reduction likely waived |
| 2 | Lakemont contract approval is not a Required Consent or closing condition | Disclosure Schedule 4.7(a), Item 3; APA §§6.5, 7.2(d) | Largest contract (~$9.4M per year) could be terminated after closing |
| 3 | Side letter renumbering moves the vehicle title rep under the cap | Side letter §2.2; APA §9.5(b) | Title claims limited to $3.85M, subject to the basket and an 18-month survival period |
| 4 | Retained License to RouteLattice is freely assignable | IPAA §7.2 | Core routing platform could pass to a competitor |
| 5 | Delaware law and forum displace New York law and forum for IP disputes | IPAA §8.1; APA §11.12 | Disputes split across two forums under two bodies of law |

The press release and board consent raise no separate legal issues. I note one related board-approval point in Part B.

---

## A. Issues

### Issue 1: Fleet Defect Notice delivered after the APA §6.8 deadline

**Location:** Side letter (October 9, 2026), Section 3, read with APA Section 6.8(b)–(d).

**What the documents say:**

- APA §6.8(b) allows Brouviv to deliver a Fleet Defect Notice "no later than 30 days after Seller delivers the Fleet Condition Report."
- APA §6.8(c) allows a price reduction only for a "timely" notice.
- Under §6.8(d), failure to deliver the notice within that period "constitutes an irrevocable waiver" of any price reduction.
- Side letter §3.1 records that Droureil delivered the Fleet Condition Report on **August 28, 2026**. The 30-day window therefore closed on **September 27, 2026**.
- Side letter §3.2 records that Brouviv delivered its notice on **October 2, 2026**. That is **five days late**. The notice covers 11 buses and claims a **$612,000** reduction.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**

- Side letter §3.3 does not cure the late delivery. It records only that the reduction is "Buyer's position." It then says the parties will resolve the notice "in accordance with Section 6.8 of the Agreement."
- That language brings in the timeliness requirement and the irrevocable-waiver language of §6.8(d). It does not waive them.
- Droureil has not conceded the reduction. On the documents as they stand, Droureil can refuse the $612,000 reduction at closing. It can also argue that it has no obligation to repair the 11 buses before closing.
- Brouviv would then be left with a post-closing indemnity claim for breach of the §4.10 condition representation. That claim is subject to the $192,500 basket in §9.4, and Droureil would argue that Brouviv's knowledge or the waiver bars it.
- Closing has not occurred, so Brouviv still has leverage to fix this.

**Recommendation:**

1. Before closing, obtain a signed amendment under APA §11.3. It should do one of the following:
   - (a) expressly waive the §6.8(b) deadline for the October 2 notice and deem the notice timely for all purposes of §6.8(c), keeping the independent repair-facility mechanism for any dispute over the estimate; or
   - (b) better, fix an agreed price reduction (for example, $612,000, or a negotiated figure) unless Droureil completes the repairs to Brouviv's reasonable satisfaction before closing.
2. Confirm whether the side letter has been countersigned. If it has not, do not countersign §3 in its current form.
3. If Droureil refuses, consider using the Lakemont gap (Issue 2) and the cap issue (Issue 3) as negotiating leverage. Brouviv can also confirm through diligence whether the 11 buses meet the §4.10 standard. If they do not, the §7.2(a) bring-down condition may not be satisfied.
4. As a process point, docket all contractual notice deadlines on receipt for the remainder of the deal.

---

### Issue 2: Lakemont contract requires Board of Education approval, but the APA does not require Droureil to obtain it

**Location:** Disclosure Schedule 4.7(a), Item 3 (quoting Section 14 of the Lakemont contract), and Schedule 4.3, read with APA Sections 6.5 and 7.2(d).

**What the documents say:**

- The Lakemont Union Free School District contract is Brouviv's largest acquired contract: **58 routes**, about **$9.4 million** in annual revenue.
- Section 14 of that contract bars any assignment or transfer "including by sale of substantially all assets, merger or change in control, without the prior written approval of the Board of Education."
- Any transfer made without that approval is void, and the District may terminate the contract.
- Schedule 4.3 confirms that the Lakemont contract (Item 3) is subject to its assignment provisions.
- APA §7.2(d) conditions Brouviv's obligation to close only on the consents of the **Ashfield Central School District and the Pell Hollow City School District**.
- APA §6.5 defines the "Required Consents" by reference to the counterparties identified in §7.2(d). Droureil's efforts covenant therefore does not cover Lakemont either.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**

- This asset sale squarely triggers Lakemont's approval right.
- As drafted, Droureil has no contractual obligation to seek Board of Education approval. Brouviv also cannot refuse to close if the approval has not been obtained.
- Brouviv could pay the full $38.5 million and then have the Lakemont contract voided or terminated. That would cost it roughly $9.4 million per year of revenue, which is more than either contract that is actually conditioned.
- Indemnity is a weak backstop:
  - The approval requirement was disclosed in Schedules 4.3 and 4.7(a), so the §4.3 no-conflicts representation is not breached.
  - Any claim would in any event fall within the $3.85 million cap.
- The LOI (§9(c)) contemplated receipt of all school district consents "where required." The APA departed from that.
- Lakemont's current term runs only to June 30, 2027, and renewal is at the District's election. The Board's view of Brouviv therefore matters for renewal as well as for assignment.

**Recommendation:**

1. Amend APA §7.2(d), and through it §6.5, to add the **prior written approval of the Lakemont Union Free School District Board of Education** as a Required Consent and closing condition. The approval should be in form reasonably satisfactory to Brouviv.
2. Ensure that §3.2(f) closing deliverables pick this up.
3. Begin Board of Education outreach now. Board meetings run on a public calendar, and approval must be obtained before the **December 15, 2026** Outside Date. Consider whether a short Outside Date extension should be pre-negotiated.
4. If Droureil will not accept a condition, the fallback is:
   - a special, uncapped indemnity for loss of the Lakemont contract (or of its renewal) arising from the transfer;
   - a holdback or escrow sized to the contract's value; and/or
   - a price adjustment if approval is not obtained by a specified date.
5. Note that waiving a material §7.2 condition requires further approval from Brouviv's board under the board consent (§3, second resolution). Adding a condition does not.

---

### Issue 3: Side letter renumbers the vehicle title representation out of the Fundamental Representations carve-out

**Location:** Side letter Section 2.2, read with APA Section 9.5(b) (and Section 9.1).

**What the documents say:**

- APA §9.5(b) defines "Fundamental Representations" as the representations "in **Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.9**."
- Breaches of those representations are excluded from:
  - the $192,500 basket in §9.4; and
  - the 10% cap in §9.5(a), which is **$3,850,000**.
- Liability for those breaches is instead capped at the full Purchase Price.
- Under §9.1, Fundamental Representations also survive until 60 days after the statute of limitations, rather than 18 months.
- Side letter §2.2 provides that "Section 4.9 is hereby deleted in its entirety" and inserts a **new Section 4.9A** in its place. Section 4.9A extends the title representation to the six Substitute Vehicles.
- Nothing in the side letter amends §9.5(b) or deems references to Section 4.9 to include Section 4.9A.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**

- Read literally, Section 4.9 no longer exists. Section 4.9A is not a Fundamental Representation.
- Droureil's representation that it has good title to all 212 buses, free of liens and financing arrangements, is now:
  - **subject to the 10% cap** and the basket; and
  - limited to **18 months' survival**.
- Title to the fleet goes to the heart of what Brouviv is paying for. A title defect affecting even a fraction of the fleet could exceed $3.85 million, and the cap is shared with every other general representation claim.
- The side letter looks favourable to Brouviv because it extends coverage to the Substitute Vehicles, but its net effect is to weaken the protection for the entire fleet.

**Recommendation:**

Amend the side letter (or deliver a further amendment under APA §11.3) to provide that:

- (a) §9.5(b) reads "Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.9A";
- (b) every reference in the APA (including §§9.1 and 9.5) to Section 4.9 is deemed a reference to Section 4.9A; and
- (c) Section 4.9A is a Fundamental Representation for all purposes.

A simpler alternative is to restate §4.9 in place, as amended, rather than deleting and renumbering it. Do not let Brouviv countersign the side letter, if it has not already done so, until this is fixed.

---

### Issue 4: Droureil can assign the RouteLattice Retained License freely, including to a competitor

**Location:** IP Assignment Agreement, Section 7.2 (read with Sections 4.1–4.5).

**What the documents say:**

- IPAA §4.1 grants Droureil a non-exclusive, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license (the **Retained License**) to use, reproduce and modify the RouteLattice Software for the Retained Charter Business.
- §4.5 lets Droureil keep a copy of the **source code**.
- §4.3 gives Droureil ownership of its own improvements.
- §7.2 allows Droureil to assign the IPAA and the Retained License "in whole or in part, **without the consent of Assignee**, to any Affiliate or to **any successor to all or any part of its business**." The only requirement is notice within 30 days *after* the assignment.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**

- RouteLattice is the routing and dispatch platform Brouviv is buying for its school bus operations. The press release describes it as strengthening routing "across our combined operations."
- Under §7.2, Droureil could sell a small piece of its charter business, or an affiliate, to a competing school bus contractor, and transfer a full source-code license with it.
- Once the license is in a competitor's hands, the field-of-use limit is weak protection:
  - Brouviv would have to detect any misuse and then enforce against it.
  - An assignee taking "part of" the business can argue the field covers whatever it acquired.
- The protections elsewhere in the deal do not reach this:
  - The APA's non-compete (§6.6) binds only Droureil and its Affiliates, not a third-party assignee.
  - The APA's anti-assignment clause (§11.5) applies only to assignment of the APA itself. It does not restrict assignment of the IPAA or the Retained License.
  - Under APA §11.12, the IPAA controls with respect to the Transferred IP in any event.
- As a result, nothing in the deal documents restricts this transfer.

**Recommendation:**

Revise IPAA §7.2 (the IPAA is still an unsigned form exhibit, so it can be negotiated now) so that:

- (a) any assignment or transfer of the Retained License, including by merger, change of control or operation of law, requires **Brouviv's prior written consent**;
- (b) the only permitted exception, if any, is an assignment to a bona fide acquirer of **all or substantially all** of the Retained Charter Business, as a whole, with prior written notice;
- (c) assignment or sublicensing to any Person that provides, or is affiliated with a provider of, **pupil transportation services** is prohibited outright;
- (d) the license is personal to Droureil and limited to the Retained Charter Business as conducted at closing;
- (e) any purported transfer in breach is void and is a ground for termination of the license, which requires carving back the "irrevocable" language in §4.1; and
- (f) source-code access is restricted, for example by retaining object code only or using named-personnel controls, with return or destruction obligations on termination.

---

### Issue 5: Delaware law and forum in the IP Assignment Agreement override New York for IP-related disputes

**Location:** IP Assignment Agreement, Section 8.1, read with APA Section 11.12 (and APA Sections 11.8 and 11.9).

**What the documents say:**

- IPAA §8.1 applies **Delaware law** and the exclusive jurisdiction of the **Delaware Court of Chancery** to any dispute "arising out of or relating to this Agreement **or the Transferred IP**."
- The APA chooses **New York law** (§11.8) and the exclusive jurisdiction of the **state or federal courts in New York County** (§11.9).
- Under the APA's order of precedence (**§11.12**), the APA controls over the Ancillary Agreements, except that the **IP Assignment Agreement controls with respect to the Transferred IP**.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**

- Because of the §11.12 carve-out, the Delaware clause prevails for any dispute touching the Transferred IP. That potentially includes:
  - claims under the APA's IP representation (§4.8);
  - related indemnity claims under Article IX; and
  - enforcement of the license-back and confidentiality terms.
- All other APA claims must be brought in New York County under New York law.
- A single post-closing dispute could therefore be split across **two forums** applying two bodies of law. For example, a claim that RouteLattice infringes third-party rights, combined with title or contract claims, could be divided in this way. The consequences for Brouviv are:
  - duplicated cost;
  - risk of inconsistent rulings; and
  - room for Droureil to argue about which court has exclusive jurisdiction.
- The arrangement is also inconsistent with:
  - LOI §8.3, under which the parties contemplated that all Definitive Agreements would be governed by New York law;
  - the Bill of Sale (§§7.2–7.3); and
  - the side letter (§5.1), both of which use New York law and forum.

**Recommendation (either fix works; ideally do both):**

- (a) Conform IPAA §8.1 to New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New York County, consistent with APA §§11.8–11.9. Federal courts in New York County can hear any copyright claims.
- (b) Amend APA §11.12 so that the IPAA's precedence for the Transferred IP covers only the terms of the conveyance and license. The carve-out should expressly **not** extend to:
  - governing law;
  - forum or jurisdiction; or
  - the APA's representations, warranties and indemnification provisions.

  This is consistent with IPAA §6.2, which already says the IPAA does not limit or expand the APA's representations or indemnities.

---

## B. Other Observations

- **Board approval of amendments.** The board consent authorizes officers to sign changes "not materially adverse to the Company." It requires further board approval for any waiver of a material §7.2 condition. If Brouviv agrees to any fallback on Lakemont that amounts to waiving that consent, or accepts the side letter's cap consequence, the officers should consider whether further board approval is needed.
- **Side letter execution status.** The copy in the folder is unsigned. We should confirm whether Brouviv has countersigned. If it has not, §§2.2 and 3.3 should be revised before signature, as described in Issues 1 and 3.
- **Bill of Sale.** The form ties the bus list to Schedule 2.1(a) "as in effect on the Closing Date," which correctly picks up the Substitute Vehicles. I found no issues with it.
- **Press release.** It is consistent with the deal terms. It refers to consents from "certain school districts," which is another reason to fix Lakemont before closing.

## C. Recommended Next Steps (before the December 15 Outside Date)

1. **This week:** Send Droureil a mark-up/amendment covering:
   - the deemed-timely Fleet Defect Notice or a fixed price reduction (Issue 1);
   - the Lakemont Required Consent and closing condition (Issue 2);
   - the §4.9A fix to §9.5(b) (Issue 3); and
   - the revised IPAA §§7.2 and 8.1 and APA §11.12 (Issues 4 and 5).
2. **Immediately:** Coordinate with Droureil on a submission to the Lakemont Board of Education, and identify the Board's next meeting date.
3. Confirm the signature status of the side letter, and hold Brouviv's countersignature pending fixes.
4. Assess whether an Outside Date extension is needed if Lakemont approval cannot be obtained in time.
5. Brief management on any changes requiring board approval.

I am happy to prepare the draft amendment and the revised IPAA.

## Issue 1: Fleet Defect Notice Was Delivered Outside the 30-Day Window

**Location:** Side letter, Section 3 (Sections 3.1–3.3); APA, Section 6.8(b) and (d).

**What the documents say:**
- **APA Section 6.8(b)** lets Buyer deliver a Fleet Defect Notice "no later than 30 days after Seller delivers the Fleet Condition Report."
- **APA Section 6.8(d)** says that failing to deliver the notice within that period "constitutes an irrevocable waiver" of any Purchase Price reduction under Section 6.8.
- **Side letter Section 3.1** records that Seller delivered the Fleet Condition Report on **August 28, 2026**. The 30-day window therefore closed on **September 27, 2026**.
- **Side letter Section 3.2** records that Brouviv delivered its Fleet Defect Notice on **October 2, 2026**. That is **five days late**. The notice covers 11 buses and a $612,000 estimated repair cost.
- **Side letter Section 3.3** states only Brouviv's *position* that the price should drop by $612,000. It then provides that the parties will resolve the notice "in accordance with Section 6.8 of the Agreement."

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**
- The side letter does not waive or extend the deadline. By incorporating Section 6.8, it arguably imports the Section 6.8(d) waiver.
- Droureil has a strong argument that Brouviv irrevocably waived the $612,000 reduction. Section 6.8(c) also reduces the price only for a "timely" notice.
- Side letter Section 3.4, which gives access to verify repairs, does not help. Droureil can simply decline to repair and decline to reduce the price.
- After closing, the reduction cannot be recovered through Section 6.8. Brouviv would have to fall back on a Section 4.10 vehicle condition claim under Article IX. That claim is subject to the $192,500 basket and the $3,850,000 cap, and Droureil will argue the defects were disclosed.
- Because Droureil signed a document recording both dates, it can point to its own record of the late delivery.

**Recommendation:**
1. Before closing, obtain a written amendment under APA Section 11.3, signed by Droureil, that does one of the following:
   - **(a)** fixes a **$612,000 Purchase Price reduction** (or a negotiated figure) at closing, regardless of Section 6.8; or
   - **(b)** expressly waives the Section 6.8(b) deadline for the October 2, 2026 notice, deems that notice "timely" for Section 6.8(c), and disapplies Section 6.8(d).
2. If Droureil refuses, consider making completion of the repairs to Brouviv's reasonable satisfaction a negotiated closing deliverable. As a fallback, consider a specific indemnity for the 11 identified buses that sits outside the basket and cap.
3. Do not make any statement that treats the notice as timely without reserving rights. Internally, assume the reduction is lost unless it is secured in writing.
4. Confirm whether the side letter has been countersigned. If it has not, revise Section 3.3 before Brouviv signs.

---

## Issue 2: Lakemont Board of Education Approval Is Not a Required Consent or Closing Condition

**Location:** Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.7(a), Item 3 (Lakemont Union Free School District); APA Sections 6.5 and 7.2(d). See also Disclosure Schedule, Schedule 4.3.

**What the documents say:**
- **Schedule 4.7(a), Item 3** discloses the Lakemont Pupil Transportation Contract:
  - 58 routes and about **$9.4 million** in annual revenue, the largest contract being acquired;
  - term ending June 30, 2027, with three one-year extensions at the District's election.
- Lakemont's contract, Section 14, bars any assignment or transfer "including by sale of substantially all assets, merger or change in control, without the prior written approval of the Board of Education." It also states that an unapproved transfer is **void**, and that the District **may terminate** on notice.
- **APA Section 6.5** obliges Droureil to seek only the consents of the counterparties "identified in Section 7.2(d)."
- **APA Section 7.2(d)** names only the **Ashfield Central School District** and the **Pell Hollow City School District**.
- **Schedule 4.3** discloses that Items 1–3 need consent. That disclosure qualifies Droureil's no-conflicts representation in APA Section 4.3.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**
- The asset sale squarely triggers Lakemont's approval right. Droureil has no covenant to obtain that approval, and Brouviv has no closing condition protecting it.
- Brouviv could be obliged to close, pay the full $38.5M, and then receive a void assignment of its largest contract, or face termination by the District.
- Lakemont accounts for roughly a third of the acquired pupil transportation revenue and more than a quarter of the routes. It also drives the need for many of the buses, drivers and depot capacity being bought.
- Because Schedule 4.3 discloses the consent requirement, Brouviv probably has **no indemnity claim** under Section 4.3 if Lakemont withholds approval.
- Failure to obtain approval is unlikely to be a Material Adverse Effect under Section 7.2(f), since the requirement was known and disclosed at signing.
- The LOI (Section 9(c)) contemplated receipt of *all* required school district consents as a condition. The APA departs from that.
- The contract term ends June 30, 2027. Brouviv also needs comfort on extension or rebid, but the approval point comes first.

**Recommendation:**
1. Amend APA Section 7.2(d) (and therefore Section 6.5) to add the **Lakemont Union Free School District Board of Education approval** as a Required Consent and a closing condition. Require the approval to be in form reasonably satisfactory to Brouviv.
2. Begin Board of Education engagement immediately. Boards act at scheduled public meetings, so the timing against the **December 15, 2026 Outside Date** is tight. Get the District's meeting calendar now and prepare Brouviv's fleet, safety and insurance package under Section 6.5.
3. If approval cannot be obtained before December 15, the options are:
   - **(a)** agree with Droureil to extend the Outside Date;
   - **(b)** negotiate a special indemnity plus escrow or holdback, sized to the value of the Lakemont contract, covering any termination or refusal of approval; or
   - **(c)** negotiate a price adjustment mechanism if Lakemont is excluded.
4. Any decision to close without Lakemont approval should go back to the Brouviv Board, consistent with Section 3 of the board consent.

---

## Issue 3: Side Letter Renumbering Takes the Vehicle Title Representation Out of the Cap Carve-Out

**Location:** Side letter, Section 2.2; APA Section 9.5(b). See also APA Sections 9.1 and 9.4.

**What the documents say:**
- **APA Section 9.5(b)** defines "Fundamental Representations" by section number as "**Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.9**." It exempts them from both:
  - the $192,500 basket (Section 9.4); and
  - the 10% cap of **$3,850,000** (Section 9.5(a)).

  Their liability is capped instead at the full Purchase Price.
- **APA Section 9.1** gives Fundamental Representations survival until 60 days after the statute of limitations. All other representations survive 18 months.
- **Side letter Section 2.2** provides that "**Section 4.9 is hereby deleted** in its entirety" and inserts a "**new Section 4.9A**" covering title to Purchased Vehicles and the six Substitute Vehicles.
- Nothing in the side letter amends Section 9.5(b). Nothing deems references to Section 4.9 to refer to Section 4.9A.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**
- On its face, the title representation for all 212 buses now sits in a section that is **not** a Fundamental Representation.
- A title defect would therefore be:
  - subject to the $3,850,000 cap, shared with every other general rep claim;
  - subject to the $192,500 basket; and
  - limited to the 18-month survival period.
- Before the side letter, such a defect was uncapped up to the Purchase Price and survived for the limitations period.
- Title to the fleet is central to the deal. The fleet is a large share of value, and it has a disclosed financing history: Depot 1 has a mortgage to Hudson Commerce Bank, and vehicle liens are not ruled out by the schedules.
- The side letter looks favourable because it extends the rep to the Substitute Vehicles. In practice it materially weakens Brouviv's protection.

**Recommendation:**
1. Amend the side letter (or sign a further amendment under APA Section 11.3) to:
   - **(a)** amend Section 9.5(b) to read "Sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.9A"; and
   - **(b)** add a general clause that every reference in the APA and the Ancillary Agreements to "Section 4.9" means Section 4.9A.
2. A simpler alternative is to restore Section 4.9 as amended, rather than deleting it and creating a new 4.9A.
3. Confirm that Sections 9.1 (survival), 9.4 (basket) and 9.5 all pick up the revised reference.
4. Separately, the Substitute Vehicle VINs in Annex A and the Removed Vehicle item numbers are still blank. Complete them before signing or closing, so that Schedule 2.1(a) and the Bill of Sale (Section 2.1(a)) cover the correct 212 buses.

---

## Issue 4: Delaware Law and Forum in the IP Assignment Agreement Override the APA's New York Provisions

**Location:** IP Assignment Agreement, Section 8.1; APA Section 11.12. See also APA Sections 11.8 and 11.9, and LOI Section 8.3.

**What the documents say:**
- **IP Assignment Agreement Section 8.1** applies "the laws of the State of Delaware" to any claim "arising out of or relating to this Agreement **or the Transferred IP**." It also submits those claims to the exclusive jurisdiction of the "**Delaware Court of Chancery**."
- **APA Sections 11.8 and 11.9** apply New York law, with exclusive jurisdiction in the state or federal courts in New York County, to all claims relating to the APA.
- **APA Section 11.12 (Order of Precedence)** makes the APA control over Ancillary Agreements, "except that the IP Assignment Agreement **shall control with respect to the Transferred IP**." Under the APA's order of precedence, the IP Assignment Agreement therefore controls over the APA for anything concerning the Transferred IP.
- **LOI Section 8.3** contemplated New York law for all Definitive Agreements. The Bill of Sale (Sections 7.2 and 7.3) follows New York law and forum.

**Why it matters for Brouviv:**
- Read together, Sections 8.1 and 11.12 let the Delaware clause govern any dispute touching the RouteLattice software, route data or marks. That arguably includes claims under the APA's IP representation (Section 4.8) and the related Article IX indemnity claims.
- All other APA claims stay in New York under New York law. One transaction could produce **two forums** and two governing laws.
- A single dispute, such as one combining a Section 4.8 IP breach with vehicle or contract claims, could have to be split. That raises cost, risks inconsistent rulings, and creates threshold fights over which court has jurisdiction.
- Both parties are New York entities, and the assets and operations are in New York. Delaware has no connection to the deal, and the clause departs from what was agreed in the LOI.
- The IP Assignment Agreement is still an unsigned form to be delivered at closing, so this is straightforward to fix now.

**Recommendation:**
1. Conform IP Assignment Agreement Section 8.1 to New York law and the exclusive jurisdiction of the state or federal courts in New York County, mirroring APA Sections 11.8 and 11.9 (as the Bill of Sale already does).
